blocks.x: I'll make a note to start here that we're interviewing Mr. Albert Francis at his home at 1922. Mandeville, yeah. Mandeville Street downtown New Orleans and this is Bill Russell. You made this book? I've read most of that. I thought you didn't know about Russell? No, no, that's Sam Charter's book. He's supposed to view some of the notes that Dick Allen took. Maybe if Dick ever talked to you, you might have some notes from him too in there. Do you mind giving your full name, your middle name and all? Albert F. Francis, yeah. F. Francis. And do you mind telling just when you were born and what part of town? Is it here in New Orleans? Can you give us your birth date?
I know that too.
Arnold Matoie. You heard of him? Yes. We talked to his widow and his daughter. I played with him. You played with him, Matoie. When was that?

When he left, Lloyd took his place around 1919. Is that at Com Anderson's? Yeah, right there. There on the Ramparts. Right way up. What you call him? Right there. Long time. The Woolworths is now. Right with Wade. We played there a long time. He was good, I'm telling you. But he liked.
Who else was in the band? Who else was in the band when you played? When I know him? Yes, what's on the band?

I know him, my wife, Paul and Paul Dominguez. Oh, is it violin? Yeah. It was four of us, yeah. Your wife played piano? Yeah, she died in my field. She was good. Her name was Edna Mitchell, I went by the name. She's in this book too.

Yes, I've heard of her. When did she die, by the way? What year was that about? 1942. 1942. December 10, yeah. Soon be 20 years now. Long time. Do you remember how we think of it? If you could tell us a little bit about her life. It's in this book, yeah. All them bands she played. Was she born right here too? Right here, she was good. Let me see what I can find it.

You might check on that and be sure it's all accurate. Oh yeah. They got plenty of things in this book that's wrong too. I know it. I know it. That's why I thought we better check on anything. He left here playing. I wrote it down. I got a fucking fine. He left here playing with me. I told him that he left here in 1922, but they said 23. You see why I know it? He said my wife was about to be a mother. He supposed to christendom baby. And she was born in August, 22, and left about June or July with Joe Oliver.
Yeah, I knew he went up with Oliver. Yeah. What is your birth date?
24th of March. And what year is that? 1894.
1894. And were you born right here in the middle? Right in the middle, yeah. What part of town did you come from? Downtown here?
8 Ward, yeah. This ward is, the 8 Ward. Right here.

Can you tell us anything about your family, if anyone else in your family, that is your father or any uncles or brothers or any older brothers? Anybody else that played music before you? No. No. None of them.
Outside of Franky Deuce was an off-cousin of mine. He's in his- He was a cousin, Franky Deuce.

Franky Deuce, yeah. What was your first instrument? Did you start on drums? Started on drums, yeah. Started on drums. How come you liked- Did you like drums when you were a boy? What age were you when you started?

No. Well, I was a good age. I was working, you know. Yeah. And played for the work with Slack. Mm-hmm. Probably in Bonnet Petit took me first. Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah. Well, I got more money I was making that. And the boss sent for me, so I quit. So I kept on playing. I went to the Army. I was known with Punch. You were with Punch? In the band Army, Punch.
About how old were you when you took up drums? Oh, yeah. What year would that be? Is that after the First World War? Oh, before that, before. Before the war, I think.
Yeah, about 1914, I guess.
Oh, 1914. And you remember any of the drummers when you were a boy that you used to like, that you'd listen to, or follow around on parades, or any other places you'd hear them?
Lloyd Cantrell. That's where I took lessons from him. He got a son. He got a son, but his son was a baby.
He played last night.
Lloyd, Lloyd. He played clandette now, yeah. His dad took lessons, yeah. Lloyd was small, yeah.
You played with Jim Robinson and Ernie Cagnolotti last night.
Mm-hmm.
Did you start right in with the lessons with Mr. Cantrell?
Right with Cantrell, yeah.
Do you remember anything about how he taught you, or what kind of a book he used? Oh, yeah. Did he use a book for you right away, or? Right away.
No, an imperial book.
Imperial method book. Mm-hmm. I've seen those for some instruments. I never did see it for drums. Do you happen to have any of that old music you started with? Did you ever save that?
I've been learning my grandkids. I can read anything with drums. I'm going to have some parts here.
I just wondered if you ever saved that old imperial book.

Oh, it's got a new method now. My grandkids got the book, I wanted to leave it here by his house he got it. I played with Pritchard Band, them heavy overtures, yeah. I read anything. See, before I was back with the swing, I used to like to read, played them reading all you see. Yeah, you see. After I found out Jazz had it, that's the best.
A friend of mine who is dead now from Chicago, I knew him out of Chicago, Baby Dodds, you came from here. I know Baby Dodds. And he started with the imperial method too.
I know Baby Dodds, I know when he left him. I was playing Tom Ashton, he was playing on the captain with Fate and Marble.
Oh, that's right, Johnny. He worked on the boat.
See, Lloyd was playing with him, but Lloyd left Fate, come with us. Yeah, came with you. Yeah.

Anyway, Baby said he liked that method real well. He lost his copy though. He said there were a lot of nice pictures. Yeah. Show just how to hold this stick. Yeah, I got the, yeah. And all that. I never did see a copy of that book. I still hope I'll find one.
I don't need to use them no more.
No, I guess not. I don't think it's published anymore. I tried to buy it and I couldn't.
Well, I tried. I bought my last book to teach my grandkid at, he know me good. You know Peterson? Yes. He knew me well. Yeah, Peterson. Broad Street.
Broad Street. What kind of a drum set did you have when you started? You had a full set?
Full set, yeah, full set.
Base drum and cymbals and everything?
Everything, yeah. And he met Augusta Bell, I got it sitting out. Oh, really? Yeah. You know the Black San Diego?
Yes.

Well, I used to take Augusta Bell and play the lead from the line, I'd have played them jazz pieces. Well, that's right. I'd read them violin parts. They had seven octaves, but Bell only got two and a half, I used to transport it down, yeah. Keep the ledger line, yeah. One time I was about to only read a drum to head you after Contrell died. I mean, a real one, you know, playing anything, you see.
Yeah, you really read it.
Well, you see a drummer, he don't know melody. There ain't no division, you see. Yeah, imagine.
You understand, yeah.
You read the top line as you snare, the second line as you bass, you see, yeah.
Can you tell me anything else that Contrell might have taught you? I mean, how did he go about it? Did he ever play with you at the lessons, or did he demonstrate the chords?

Yeah, you know what I used to do? He used to play in the nightclub, you know? Yeah. I used to be a scholar at the time at the nightclub. I'd say, I would play a piece of my play, and he'd sneak off. Oh, really? He'd play all night, but he'd come there to get the money.
Well, it was a good experience, but it was a good practice.
Mangan Parash, you know them fellas, they died.
I knew him, but I never did get the hearing.
Yeah.
I met him in 1943.
Yeah, he was swell. He stopped playing a long time.
Yeah, a long time ago. I never did get the hearing. Did you play with him very much?

Yeah, I played with all them bands, yeah. All in all, if you need to be sure to come get them. Yeah. But Marie would work in them nightclub, you know? Yeah. Played a regular nightclub with them regular jobs.
How long did you take lessons from Mr. Cottrell?

Not too long. Well, see, my first wife, she most enlightened me. Oh, she was the? She was a good musician, yeah. She was good. Them fellas tell you about it. She was a sight reader. She was wonderful.
Do you remember who she studied with? Did she have the...
She told me a lady she studied with, because they used to play duets together. A lady teacher. A lady teacher, yeah.
There was one Wilhelmina Bart.
I know her. She worked at Tomath with me, too. She was with you, too. Yeah, she worked at... She lived at Covington. She lived about 30 miles from there.
I met her once when Lizzie Miles was working on Bergen Street. She came by to hear Lizzie. She used to be a friend of her.

Friend of Liz. I'm a Lizzie girl. Her name was Lizzie Pazio, for you. Oh, yeah. She still uses that name. My, yeah. I know Lizzie well. Your honey Wilhelmina was well-friendly. Her name is now Wilhelmina Durone.
Durone, that's right.
Yeah, that's a maiden name Bart. Yeah, she's got a name Wilhelmina Bartchek.
Is there anything else you can tell us about your wife? That is a different band she worked in.
She played every band around that she played with. All of them. About everything.
All of them, yeah.
I met Michael Moneta at a wedding Saturday.
What was it? I saw him about a month ago. I haven't seen him for about a month.
And Bebe Ridgely, I shook hands with him at Piku's funeral.

Yeah, I didn't see him. I was there at the funeral, but I didn't see him. They had a picture of him in the paper there. And he died about a month, a couple months later, too. Yeah. Did you ever work with Bebe? I guess you did. With Bebe. Bebe Ridgely?
Oh, yeah. And that tuxedo, all of them, yeah. Celestat's voice. Paul Barnes, too. Yeah. Yeah.
What was your very first band then, after you started out?
Well, my first band was named, we had a fella by the name of Thomas Copeland, Maurice Duran.
What did Copeland play? I knew him.
He used to play bass, Thomas Copeland.
I knew Maurice Duran, he was a trumpet player.

Yeah, the clarinet player was named, he died, too. And the bass, the banjo player was named Bernard, Charlie Bernard. Yeah. I can't think of the clarinet player name, good as I know him, too. All of them is dead, all of them. Maurice was living there. Yeah, Maurice. He was down there when Ricard died.
Yeah. And he was in San Francisco, I guess, when he died there.
Yeah. Yeah, Joe Watson, the clarinet player. Oh, Joe Watson.
Joe Watson. Yeah, I've seen a picture of him.
Yeah, Joe Watson.
I believe it was, maybe Camellia Band or some...
That's the band that Milly Bond had, Camellia Band. But before that, it wasn't a Camellia Band.
It wasn't, I don't remember a word, but...
Then I left, I went to San Luis, but I wasn't playing up there. And I got drafted on me up there, around 1916, 17.

Is there anything else you can think of about your wife? I don't like to keep bothering you about... Oh, that's all right. ...since she isn't here, if there's anything else you could add about her life and the style of piano that she played.
Well, she played both kinds, she was wonderful. She played a lot of solo.
She was side-wheeling, then she could change keys, yeah.
She was wonderful. All them bands, she'd play, so come get all of them.
In those days, did the pianist ever take many solos?
They do it, no, take hops.
Of course, nowadays, they take a solo, everybody takes a solo after that.
Yeah, she was wonderful on that. I just wondered if they did in those days. Yeah, all the same way they take... Played mostly chords and...
Yeah, no, it takes solos.
It takes solos in, too.
What about drum solos? When did they come in?

Well, I remember years ago, you couldn't hear no drum on the television, the radio. That's right, you never heard. They sure late in the style. I believe what you call them, start them fellas like Lionel Hampton and this fella.
Gene Krupa?

Gene Krupa like them, yeah, they start that, you see, yeah. And the center fella, I met Louie when he came down last time, that fella got the fun. Cozy Cole. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And the center fella, big tall fella. Sidney Catlett. Oh, yeah. He died now. Every time Louie come here, come see me, come the last one he played with us. Yeah, and this book they got him, last one he played.
That was the Tom Anderson's.
Yeah, my name, my wife's name, and Paul Dominguez. Paul is dead. We had four pieces there.

One time I saw one picture of a band there, I think Wooden Joe had that picture. Who was that? Wooden Joe Nicholas. Oh, I know Wooden Joe, yeah. With his nephew who was playing, Barney Begard and Nicholas. Albert Nicholas. Albert Nicholas.
Albert Nicholas. They was playing Tom Anderson after we left there.
After you left.
After the job, after you left. Yeah, yeah. I know Albert Nicholas.
I played many jobs with him. Oh, Willie San Diego, they had him on guitar.
He was a guitar player. Played with him too.
And I believe Paul Bartman was a drummer then after you left.
Paul Bartman, yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah. That was after our time. Yeah. We were there first.
They had a little bit bigger band. You only had four pieces there.
Four pieces, yeah. That band was larger now.
Yeah.
See that time, but after the cabaret started getting plentiful, but they had competition, you had to increase the band, you see. What kind of place was that? Did they have any shows?
No, they had entertainers. Entertainers that sang all around the same place.

Yeah, we had four people. The fellow would take and raise the music and the corner play, he played on special chorus. Played the saxophone part. We'd write a lot for him, you see, with our four pieces. Because Louie would do it too. They would get a piano part and write the whole four pieces out. Yeah. Because Paul Lomengus, he was a good reader too. I know how much why. He was first class. But many of these fellows, they couldn't read too much. Yeah. But if they hear something, they can play it good the fellow read it though. One thing about them.
A wonderful ear of some of those people.
Now Buddy Petit, well, he's time that, had about five. Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Rene, Sam Morgan. Yeah, they had the town.
You mentioned something about you worked with Buddy Petit, that's when you gave up your other job.
Yeah, first band I played in the cabaret, after I left Joe. Joe was watching them. I was playing the Poodle Dog, or Liberty and Biamma.
The Poodle Dog, yeah.
The Poodle Dog used to call it. Yeah, I never knew that Poodle Dog.
Yeah.
They had a bunch of them. 101 rank, they had a few clothes, rice, grocery, right where Krause is. Oh yes, right there. And that Krause was 25, they used bands there too.
I remember the 25. Yeah. Did you ever have bands in the 25 then? I thought it was mostly a gambling place. There was a gambling in the back, they had bands there too.

Did they have any dancing or what they played for? They had some good fellows there, like this fella, Albert Cal, I don't know much about him. Oh, piano players. Yeah, Albert Cal, Wade Martin, yeah. The great fella they had there. Used to come in with such a big town, you know.
Yeah. I was reading a little book here about the district.
This book I was reading. Show you all them fans houses too, yeah.
I was reading the show in New Orleans. The French Quarter. Yeah, everything. What kind of a place was Tom Anderson's? Was it a pretty big place at Cabaret? He was there, he had a swell place.

He had lead of the town. Anything he wanted he did there. I heard he was the boss of the district. He was great, yeah. And the way he sees place, all of all were looking glass. Anywhere you go they could see it. Oh really?
Yeah, he had a swell place, yeah.

Well years I have to give up, he had his son lost to run a father named George Delsick. Oh yeah, I heard it. Used to run it, yeah. Used to run it. I worked there a long time for him. He was a nice friend. You never know, he'd never tell the band nothing. Never tell the band nothing. They'd give you a $5 bill, but don't take a dollar for him. You had to share the straight place. He'd never say nothing.
That was Tom bootlegging time too.
Oh that's right, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. They served liquor there. Oh yeah. They'd get it for you.
Yeah. See them fellas take a milk bottle, you know, painted white, you know. Yeah. Put whiskey in there, they couldn't see if they'd take it for milk.
They did that. I never heard of that. Pretty good idea. They did that at Tom Anderson's. Right. They had some fun around there.
Yeah.
And they had entertainers like singers, you say.
Yeah, they had a singer, that's an entertainer, yeah. Yeah. Had a fella by, you know what I'd talk to him, Willie Jackson. Oh yeah.
He made some records once with the- Yeah.
Where you met him at?
I never met him, but I have some of his records.

Yeah, he left. He made some with- He was good. With Steve Lewis. Yeah, I know, I played with Steve too, but he regular band was Piron. Yeah, he played with Steve. Yeah, at Tranchinas. Yeah. And I played a long time at Club Forest up there with Duck Ones, many good fellas. See, where was the Club Forest?
Is that on Bourbon? No, I saw Metry.
Oh, Metry, yeah.
I never knew it before my time.

That was a big place, right across from my, that big gambling place. Lillen Strong played that once he came in. He did too? Yeah. That, you know, called the Beverly Garden too. Oh yeah. The Beverly Garden. Beverly Garden.
Beverly Garden. Beverly Garden. Yeah, sure, I know where it is.
We played there a long time.
To get back to Tom Anderson, did they have a dance floor for the customers to dance too? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah.
Dance floor, yeah. They had a dance floor. Nice dance floor.
Customers mostly come in just for-

Well that time they had stars then, you know, stars. Oh yeah. The man come in and see the place packed, you see. Well if the man bomb or drink, they got percentage on it, you see. They draw the man's in there. They'd be packed with girls.
They had a lot of girls around there.
Oh yeah, plenty of girls. That's all they had. Then they had a place two blocks back that's called the Annex. Yeah, yeah. Billis Studios to run that.
On Basin Street.
Yeah, Billis Studios to run that. Yeah, they had some nice clubs around there.
Yeah. When did you start working for Tom Anderson, about how early was that?
About, after about 19, last part of 1918. 1918. Yeah, like that part. Yeah.
Was the district still running pretty good then? On the slide, yeah, yeah.
Yeah. But the district closed down, a big part closed down around 15, 16. Well it closed down during the war.
When the war started, yeah, yeah.
But after the war opened, they had private houses. Yeah, they still had it.
Yeah.
Yeah. And bootleggers time, I was around 19. Yeah. You still had a chance. You still got them now, for that concern. Yeah, I guess.

Mm-hmm. I wonder if there's anything else you can tell us about the early drummers when you were a boy, even before you took up music. You mentioned, of course, your teacher, Cantrell. Cantrell. But some of the other early drummers. Walter Brunson.
Yeah.
Walter Brunson. Yeah. Baby Dodd said he used to take lessons from him. He liked him.
He was good, yeah. Well, I know him a twine, there was no read. And one named Mack Murray.
Oh, Mack Murray.
Yeah.
Well, anything about Walter Brunson? Anything else about his style? What kind of a brother?

He was wonderful. He was wonderful. Had a fella named Mack Murray, too. Yeah. Well, Barbara and I, we about to start together. Paul Barbara. Yeah, we start about together. And we had a little fella by the name of your talk, Joe Lindsey. Oh, yeah, Joe Lindsey. Yeah, we was talking at the same time. I knew him.
He was a friend of Louis Armstrong. Louis Armstrong, yeah.
Yeah, yeah. Joe Lindsey.
I met him up in Chicago. Baby Dodds. Yeah.
Hendriss Eno.
Oh, yeah, I never knew him. I heard people talking.
Yeah, he was good too, Hendriss Eno. You remember who he played with? Well, he used to play all in my club, different band. And Black, we were talking Black Benny. Yeah. Little Red Happy.
Yeah, I never knew him either. I never knew Black Benny. I heard people talking.
I know all of them. Black Benny used to come and try to get lessons from me. And Zula Singleton. He's up Zula Singleton. Yeah, they call him Zula, yeah.
I knew him in New York.
Yeah, he left here.
Well, he used to talk about the John Veen. Do you remember?
John Veen, oh, he's an old man.
Yeah.

Well, I remember I took his job. He'd sleep. He had a shop in the daytime and sleep all night. Yeah, I remember. Yeah, a long time. I had a, what you call him playing at that time too? Sidney Bechet. Sidney Bechet. I know Sidney Bechet. Well, yeah. That was one of them nightclubs, you know, then. He'd sleep all day. John Veen, he's there. He used to play bass on the parade. A bass drum. Yeah, the parade, yeah. What bands did he play with?
Well, all them bands, like Imperial Band, you know.
Yeah. Yeah. Now, you got a fella playing trombone. His brother was a drummer too. From Al Jays. They called his brother Bebe, Bill Mathias. Oh, yeah.
He had a brother play drums, Bebe.
Yeah, I heard it.
I never knew it. I know Bill. Yeah, Bill played. He used to play drum too, but he played trombone.

Yeah. Well, you already talk, that fella, Louis Double, Red Allen. Oh, yeah. I played with all them, yeah. George O'Neill. Yeah. George O'Neill, he's not here though. Now, they got an old friend of mine, he used to play violin. He used to play with Sam Morgan and them, but he stopped playing years. I know some of them old fellas too, but he stopped playing years. He's a violin player? He used to play violin, yeah. What is his name? Pete Alexander. Oh, Pete Alexander.
And I know of course Tats, Adolph Alexander, any relation to them? No, I played with Tats, but he's kind of paralyzed. Yeah, he had a sort of stroke.
I played many times with Tats, yeah. He's paralyzed now.
He was wonderful too. Yeah?
Good musician. He played baritone horn too, I know. His dad used to be a teacher. Old man Alexander. I used to play at that big band, Heard Talk of Pritchett. Yeah.
But he couldn't get them fellas to play it.
I know why they didn't want to learn you. He had a good band. It was a big brass band, wasn't it? Big brass band.
Yeah.

Big brass band. Yeah. I used to play at that big band. Heard Talk of Pritchett. Yeah. Yeah, but he couldn't get them fellas to play it. Where did they rehearse? The last play we rehearsed was at the Tulane Club. I got a picture of where you band first thought I got here.
Oh really?
I'd like to see that. Plennifeld is dead. Paggio is dead. Lange is dead. Yeah, I knew him. Ridd is dead. You know Ridd the bass player? Yeah, sure. Joseph Clark. Yeah, classic.
One of the first bands. Yeah. You know Pete Redfield? Yeah. Yeah.
You know Pete Redfield? Yeah.
Yeah. He's good too.
But he's got one leg of it. That's Pritchett's band. Yeah. That's a long time. Where was this taking that one? Looks like out in the country.
No, our Jefferson Racetrack. Oh yeah.
That's Red.
That's Albert Warne, you see? Yeah.
That's Red. Yeah, that's Red. Yeah, that's Paggio.
Oh yeah.
That's Landry, you see? That's Paggio. Oh yeah.
That's Landry, you see? That's Pritchett.
And the next is Paggio. That's Paggio.
Oh yeah.
That's Landry, you see?
That's Landry's second to the right on the back. Yeah. That's Pritchett, yeah. I'll bring my camera down someday and I'll snap a picture of this. That's Red. Yeah, that's Red. That's me, you see?
Right there. Your right, he's second to the left.
Yeah, that's my son. Your son on clarinet. Yeah.
Well, at least he gives it up. Yeah.
Remember who the other clarinets are?

That's a Jewmaker. Oh yeah. That boy's a good drummer. That's a Pete Rayfield, he got one leg on. Oh yeah, you mentioned. Yeah. Oh, I can handle them over too. He'd lift, he'd play bass drum, you know? He'd do all the fella. He'd do all the fella. That's a good drummer. That's a Pete Rayfield, he got one leg on. He'd do all the fella. I used to like him. That was the Jefferson Racetrack that was taken.
Is Pritchard down here too? That's Pritchard. That's Pritchard there.
He works in that pressing shop on Rampart Street. He's wonderful too, yeah.
He's still up there then? He's still there, yeah.
I passed there and talked to him. Rampart about a block left off Canal Street on the Riverside. On the Riverside? A place named Grisby and Grisby, pressing shop.
Grisby, I'll have to...
Yeah. He's got some girls in there playing. He's wonderful, him.
Yeah, I see a couple girls on sax. Yeah. Oh, is that Old Man Barbaran? That's Old Man Barbaran, yeah. Old Man Barbaran.
Who's the other trombonist here?
Do you know? Yeah, that's Henry.
Sonny Henry?
No, not Sonny, that's Oscar Henry.
Sonny Henry's dead. I saw him this morning by the drip hook. I saw him this morning by the drip hook. I had a bunch of one on the convention.
That's Oscar Henry?
Oscar Henry, yeah.
He looks a little different than he does now.
He's small now.
The next one is a baritone horn, I guess. That trumpet looks familiar. I can't think who it would be though.
Where?
That's Pajot. No, in front there. I don't think anybody I know.
I can't make him up.
Red was playing trombone then.
That's Red Day. I brought this fellow one night from New Huygenson, he dropped there the next night.
Landry. Landry, yeah. I remember in 1949 he was playing at the Big Eye.
That's Old, I forgot this Old Man there.
Oh, down in front there.
Old Man Delmore, he used to be a professor too. On the tuba, is that it? No, on the bass, he was sitting down by the bass, he'd just direct the band, would preach it.
Oh yeah.
I had plenty of pictures of it bands, but I got rid of them, you know.
It's too bad you didn't save some of those old bands, they're hard to find now.
Old Man Bobberant died too.
Yeah, last summer, about a year ago.

Listen, I know later now, listen, we'll tell you this now, between you and I, one of the oldest bands in town. You understand? They'd be surprised if you get this. Billy Moran, you know what I'm talking about? Billy Moran. Oh yes, the line's Moran's father. That's his daddy.
Yeah.

And there's, oh, you see, they got an old lady well, she got the picture, you see that picture, you got about five of them. Yeah, go ahead and ask him. The Imperial is the Berry. The Imperial is the Berry. Mad Press was playing with the Imperial, and Buck Jones was playing with the Superior. You already talked about that band, you already talked about that picture. I knew Buck very well. Yeah, and Walter Brunner was playing with the Imperial band, yeah. You already talked about that picture, but she said nobody get it. And she broke the diamond. You all just might go there and get a couple dollars and take it in there, you can get it out there.
So we can take a new picture from it, you know what I mean? Yeah, holy, all that shit.

I mean it's better than this, it's lifestyle. Yeah. That time they had no saxophone, they got bass, guitar, trombone, cornet, clarinet, and drum, six pieces. I mean it's a wonderful picture. It'll worth money.
When did the saxophones come into the band? Do you know about? I had a record of it.
There was a fella by the name of Saxon I believe that started that. He was gonna say it's a fake instrument.
Yeah, but when did they start using them here in the city?

I know it was way late in the 1900 I know. Yeah, way late in the 1900 they started that, I'm sure of that. I remember when I first started the clarinet play, they had two clarinets, you remember that? Yeah. They had a car A and a B.
Yeah. You remember that? I've seen the A clarinet.

They had a car A and a B because they couldn't transport. And the cornet with that short they had put them bits on there, remember that? Yeah, I've seen those too. I remember them young boys they knowin' about that. And if anybody told you about Joe Petit, he used to play a vowel trumpet. I knew him, yeah.
I made a record once with him. Did you? He played at that time on the slide.
The slide and he had a key trumpet on there for you.
He didn't have any teeth when he made this record. No teeth. No teeth at all. Yeah, he's a nice old man. Who was playing the corner?
No, but when I heard him though, he had given up music.
